title: When the Hymn Burns
premise: Urban explorer Dominic Blackwood has spent five years documenting the Hollowmere tunnels—passages that appear on no survey and hum with a hymn only they can hear. When their childhood imaginary friend, a frost-pale figure called Wren, appears on their porch unchanged after twenty-five years, Dominic learns the truth: as a child they stole a votive offering from the thing beneath the town, and every disappearance since 1974 has been a payment on their debt. As winter's first frost begins writing a pattern across the town that mirrors the tunnels below, Dominic must descend with Wren, return what was taken, and choose between their own survival and the town's. In the end, Dominic gives back the offering and takes Wren's place as the hymn's keeper—until the final chapter reveals the pattern has begun again, on someone else's porch.
about_author: Noor Villalobos is a former municipal archivist from upstate New York who spent a decade cataloguing property records for towns that no longer exist. Their fiction blends bureaucratic dread with folk horror, and they claim to have never explored a tunnel they weren't invited into.

chapters.title: The Survey That Doesn't Exist
chapters.summary: Dominic, in first person, maps a newly opened section of the Hollowmere tunnels and records a hymn-like hum their equipment can't source. They tell themselves it's water pressure. The chapter establishes their ritualized rationality and ends with a chalk mark on the tunnel wall that matches marks from their childhood home. Beat: uneasy denial.

chapters.title: What the Frost Knows
chapters.summary: Dominic returns to their apartment to find frost patterns on every window despite it being October—each pattern identical to their childhood bedroom's. POV stays with Dominic. A neighbor mentions the town's 1974 disappearances for the first time. Beat: the past pressing through the present's seams.

chapters.title: Wren, Unchanged
chapters.summary: Dominic wakes to find Wren—the frost-pale imaginary friend they invented at age six—sitting on the porch, exactly as remembered. Wren speaks only in the hymn's melody and one sentence: 'You still have it.' Dominic's carefully built adult identity cracks. Beat: terror braided with terrible nostalgia.

chapters.title: The 1974 File
chapters.summary: Dominic raids the county archive, where a sympathetic clerk, Marisol, lets them see sealed records: nine children vanished in 1974, all from one street—Dominic's. The file includes a photograph of a votive object that Dominic recognizes instantly. Beat: the rational framework collapses into evidence.

chapters.title: Mother's Silence
chapters.summary: Dominic confronts their mother, Eleanor, whose dementia flickers into horrifying clarity: she remembers 1974, remembers what Dominic carried home from the woods, remembers the bargain the parents made. She begs Dominic to leave town before the frost completes. Beat: inherited guilt, the price of parental protection.

chapters.title: Nine Names
chapters.summary: Marisol joins the investigation, and they identify the nine vanished children—some were Wren's 'friends' too. Each child's family suffered a frost-pattern death within a year. Dominic realizes they were the tenth child, the one who took instead of gave. Beat: survivor's guilt weaponized.

chapters.title: The Hymn Has Words
chapters.summary: Dominic dreams the hymn with lyrics for the first time: an accounting song, itemizing what was taken and what is owed. They wake with frost on their tongue. Wren waits at the foot of the bed, patient, and points toward the tunnel entrance under the old church. Beat: the debt becomes personal and urgent.

chapters.title: Descent, First Attempt
chapters.summary: Dominic enters the tunnels with Marisol but turns back when the passages begin repeating their own childhood home's layout in miniature. Marisol hears her dead brother's voice in the hum and has to be dragged out. Beat: the tunnels as mirror, not maze.

chapters.title: What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Eleanor, lucid for one long evening, tells the full story: in 1974 the town fed something beneath Hollowmere a votive of woven hair and teeth, and ten-year-old Dominic pried it from the stone and kept it. The disappearances stopped—but the thing began collecting interest. Beat: the protagonist's complicity fully revealed.

chapters.title: The Object
chapters.summary: Dominic opens the locked tin they've carried through five moves without ever examining: the votive, still cold, still faintly singing. Touching it, they experience flashes of the thing below—its patience, its hunger, its strange tenderness toward children. Beat: horror laced with unwanted empathy.

chapters.title: Frost Line
chapters.summary: The frost patterns complete across town, tracing the tunnel map exactly. Three residents vanish overnight; the town blames a gas leak. Dominic, watching the pattern from a water tower, understands the final frost line points at their apartment door. Beat: deadline made visible.

chapters.title: Justice Outside the Law
chapters.summary: Dominic tries to confess to the police and is nearly committed; the town's institutions are complicit, built on the 1974 bargain. Marisol proposes they stop asking permission: gather the descendants of the nine families and go down together. Beat: the turn from victim to actor.

chapters.title: The Descendants
chapters.summary: Seven descendants answer the call in Marisol's garage. Each carries a fragment—letters, a recording of the hymn, a child's drawing of Wren. Old resentments flare: some want the debt paid, some want the thing destroyed, one wants Dominic handed over. Beat: fragile coalition, competing justices.

chapters.title: Wren's Testimony
chapters.summary: Wren appears to the group and, through Marisol's recorder, tells what it is: not the thing below, but the thing's outstretched hand—sent to children because children could carry what adults couldn't. It has waited twenty-five years not as a debt collector but as a guide. Beat: the imaginary friend recontextualized.

chapters.title: The Church Basement
chapters.summary: The group enters through the sealed church basement. The tunnels now show them their own worst memories rendered in frost and stone. One descendant, Ruthie, walks into a wall of her grandmother's grief and is lost to the pattern. Beat: first real loss, stakes made flesh.

chapters.title: The Accounting Room
chapters.summary: They reach a cavern where the walls are inscribed with every transaction since 1830—the town's whole history written in offerings. Dominic finds their own entry, the only one left open. The hum here is deafening, and the hymn finally resolves into a question: what will you return? Beat: awe and dread fused.

chapters.title: The Bargain Refused
chapters.summary: The thing below offers Dominic the old deal: give back the votive and walk away, debt closed, town doomed to keep paying in children. Dominic, remembering the nine names and Ruthie, refuses the terms. The frost begins closing in. Beat: the moral climax—survival rejected as insufficient.

chapters.title: What Dominic Owes
chapters.summary: Dominic realizes the votive was never the true debt—the debt is the life the town bought with it, the life Dominic has lived on stolen credit. Wren offers to take their place, as it always meant to. Dominic refuses that too. Beat: the protagonist chooses consequence over escape.

chapters.title: The Return
chapters.summary: Dominic returns the votive and then offers themselves as the new keeper of the accounting—the one who remembers all the names, who keeps the hymn honest so it needn't hunt. The thing accepts. The frost patterns across town melt into harmless rime. Beat: sacrifice as restitution, not martyrdom.

chapters.title: Above Ground
chapters.summary: Marisol and the descendants surface to a town that remembers nothing and a Dominic who stands at the tunnel mouth, changed—older, translucent at the edges, singing under their breath. Eleanor, lucid, tells them she's proud. Beat: grief and grace, the price made visible to those who stay.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Hymn
chapters.summary: Dominic, in the tunnels, learns the work: listening, recording, ensuring every offering is freely given. They and Wren walk the passages together, keeper and guide. Dominic narrates with new clarity—no longer explaining the noises, but conducting them. Beat: reconciliation with the monstrous and the self.

chapters.title: Someone Else's Porch
chapters.summary: Years later, in a distant town, a child's imaginary friend sits on a porch, unchanged, patient. The child's mother, an archivist, finds a survey of tunnels that appear on no map—with a dedication in Dominic's hand: 'Return what was taken. It will wait, but not forever.' Beat: the cycle continues, watchful rather than cruel.
